stem: Which pair of travelling waves can produce a stable standing wave through superposition?
options: Waves of equal frequency and amplitude moving in opposite directions
Waves of different frequencies moving in the same direction
Waves of different speeds and amplitudes moving in opposite directions
Waves of equal frequency moving in the same direction
explanation: Two waves with equal frequency, wavelength and amplitude travelling in opposite directions can interfere to form a stable standing-wave pattern.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: What is the separation of two adjacent displacement nodes in a standing wave of wavelength λ?
explanation: Adjacent displacement nodes are separated by half a wavelength.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: A string fixed at both ends has length 0.90 m and vibrates in the pattern shown. What is the wavelength of the travelling waves that form this standing wave?
explanation: Three half-wavelengths fit the string: L = 3λ/2. Hence λ = 2(0.90)/3 = 0.60 m.
diagramAlt: A standing wave on a string fixed at each end shows three loops across a length of 0.90 m.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: A string is fixed at its left end and free at its right end. The string is 0.40 m long and waves on it travel at 120 m s⁻¹. What is the first-harmonic frequency?
explanation: The fixed end is a displacement node and the free end an antinode, so L = λ/4. The first-harmonic frequency is v/(4L) = 120/1.60 = 75 Hz.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: Two adjacent antinodes on a standing wave are separated by one node. What is their phase difference?
explanation: The displacement oscillations in adjacent loops are in antiphase, giving a phase difference of π radians.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: P and Q are two positions strictly between the same pair of neighbouring nodes of a standing wave. How do their oscillations compare?
options: They have the same amplitude and opposite phase.
They have the same frequency and phase, but may have different amplitudes.
They have different frequencies but the same phase.
They have the same frequency and always opposite phase.
explanation: All non-node points in one loop oscillate in phase with the same frequency. Their amplitudes vary with position.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: The displacement standing-wave pattern shown is established in an air column closed at one end and open at the other. The length is 0.75 m and the speed of sound is 300 m s⁻¹. What is the frequency?
explanation: The diagram contains three quarter-wavelengths: L = 3λ/4. Therefore f = 3v/(4L) = (3 × 300)/(4 × 0.75) = 300 Hz.
diagramAlt: A closed-open air column shows three quarter-wavelengths, with the closed end a displacement node and the open end an antinode.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: A pipe open at both ends is 0.80 m long. The speed of sound is 320 m s⁻¹. What is the first-harmonic frequency?
explanation: For an open-open pipe, the first harmonic has L = λ/2, so f = v/(2L) = 320/1.60 = 200 Hz.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the displacement of air at the ends of a pipe that is closed at both ends?
options: There is a displacement antinode at each end.
One end is a displacement node and the other an antinode.
There is a displacement node at each end.
Neither end can be a node.
explanation: Air cannot move longitudinally at a rigidly closed end, so both closed ends are displacement nodes.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: A mechanical oscillator is driven by an external periodic force. Under which condition is its steady-state amplitude generally greatest when damping is small?
options: When the driving frequency is close to its natural frequency
When the driving frequency is zero
When the driving frequency is much higher than its natural frequency
When the driving period is always twice its natural period
explanation: For weak damping, the largest forced oscillation occurs when the driving frequency is close to the natural frequency.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: A string fixed at both ends produces its first harmonic at 85 Hz. What is the frequency of its fourth harmonic if the wave speed remains unchanged?
explanation: For a string with two fixed ends, fn = n f1. Thus f4 = 4 × 85 = 340 Hz.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: A standing wave on a string has the pattern shown. What is the phase difference between the oscillations of particles P and Q?
explanation: P and Q lie in the first and third loops. Across two intervening nodes the phase reverses twice, so these loops oscillate in phase.
diagramAlt: A third-harmonic standing wave with points P and Q marked in the first and third antinodes.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: An air column closed at one end has a first-harmonic frequency of 90 Hz. Which other frequency can form a standing wave in the same air column?
explanation: A closed-open air column supports only odd multiples of its first harmonic: 90, 270, 450, ... Hz. Among the options only 270 Hz is allowed.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: Two counter-propagating sound waves establish a standing wave in air. Consecutive displacement antinodes are 0.85 m apart. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What is the frequency of either travelling wave?
explanation: The antinode separation is λ/2 = 0.85 m, hence λ = 1.70 m. f = 340/1.70 = 200 Hz.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: A door closer returns the door to its equilibrium position as rapidly as possible without oscillating. Which type of damping best describes this behaviour?
explanation: Critical damping is the fastest return to equilibrium without oscillation.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: The graph shows amplitude against driving frequency for two oscillators with different amounts of damping. Which statement is supported by the curves?
options: Oscillator A has more damping than B.
Both have exactly the same damping.
Oscillator B has more damping than A.
Oscillator B must have a greater maximum driving force.
explanation: Increased damping lowers and broadens the resonance peak. Curve B is broader and lower than A, so B has greater damping.
diagramAlt: Two amplitude versus driving frequency curves: A is a tall narrow peak, B is a lower broad peak.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: A mass–spring oscillator is damped more strongly but is still able to oscillate. How does its resonance response to an identical sinusoidal driving force generally change?
options: The resonance peak becomes lower and broader.
The resonance peak becomes higher and narrower.
The amplitude becomes independent of driving frequency.
explanation: Increasing damping reduces the maximum forced amplitude and typically broadens the response, making resonance less sharply defined.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: Which application deliberately uses resonance to produce a large amplitude of vibration?
options: A vehicle shock absorber suppressing oscillations
A car windscreen laminated to resist cracking
A swing pushed at regular intervals matching its natural period
A door closer returning without overshoot
explanation: A swing is driven effectively when pushes are timed near its natural frequency, increasing oscillation amplitude.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.

stem: A tube of length L is open at both ends. Another tube of the same length is closed at one end and open at the other. The speed of sound is the same in both. What is the ratio of their first-harmonic frequencies, open–open to closed–open?
explanation: Open-open first harmonic is v/(2L), whereas closed-open first harmonic is v/(4L); their frequency ratio is 2:1.
sourceNote: Original C.4 question aligned to the IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025; uploaded C.4 Paper 1A questions used as style benchmarks, not copied.
